what_it_does: Temperature sensors embedded in chips must be tiny, accurate, and stable across extreme ranges (–40 to 125 degrees Celsius). Traditional designs use active transistors, but their properties drift with temperature, requiring complex calibration. This paper presents a resistor-based approach using wire metal (a routing layer in the chip) as the sensing element. Instead of measuring resistance directly with a biasing current (which introduces error), it uses a fractional-discharge frequency-locked loop that converts temperature information into a frequency, paired with a time-domain amplifier for sensitive readout. The innovation is achieving high accuracy (±0.2 degrees Celsius) and excellent resolution figure-of-merit in an ultra-compact area, making it practical for distributed thermal monitoring in large chips.
